title: The 99% Model

scenario.situation: The fraud team has trained a new detection model that scores 99% accuracy on the holdout set. Leadership is eager to deploy it to production next sprint.
scenario.stakeholderBelief: The VP of Risk is convinced 99% accuracy proves the model is ready — 'that's better than any analyst we have.'
scenario.question: Is 99% accuracy enough evidence that this model is deployment-ready?

decisions.prompt: The VP wants sign-off by end of week. How do you frame your evaluation?

options.label: Benchmark against the VP's target accuracy
options.detail: Verify the 99% figure holds across a few slices and declare it ready if it does.
options.consequence: The 99% holds up across slices — because the model predicts 'no fraud' nearly everywhere and the dataset is 99% legitimate. You've validated the VP's belief without ever testing what the model actually catches.
options.divergenceCost: Anchored on the stakeholder's metric and never asked whether that metric measures the right thing.

options.label: Diagnostic counterfactual: compare model to a naive baseline
options.detail: Ask what a trivially dumb model (predict-never-fraud) would score, then measure the real model against that baseline on fraud-specific outcomes.
options.consequence: The naive baseline also scores 99% accuracy — instantly exposing that accuracy is not discriminating between 'great model' and 'useless model.' You now have the right thread to pull.

options.label: Run a cost-benefit analysis on deployment
options.detail: Estimate revenue impact if the model goes live, using the 99% figure as the effectiveness input.
options.consequence: Your cost-benefit looks great — because it inherits the inflated accuracy figure. You've built a rigorous-looking case on a flawed foundation.
options.divergenceCost: Jumped to business impact before validating the underlying metric.

options.label: Tune the decision threshold to maximize accuracy further
options.detail: Search for the threshold that pushes accuracy even higher before evaluating.
options.consequence: Accuracy nudges up slightly — because the optimal threshold for accuracy is to flag almost nothing as fraud. You've maximized the wrong objective and moved further from catching actual fraud.
options.divergenceCost: Optimized the wrong objective and deepened the class-imbalance blind spot.

decisions.prompt: You pull the confusion matrix. Which metric view do you trust to confirm what the model is actually doing?

artifact.title: Model performance — headline metrics
artifact.caption: All four metrics for the same model on the same holdout set. Accuracy looks excellent — but does it tell the same story as the others?

options.label: Accuracy (99.1%)
options.detail: Treat the headline accuracy figure as the primary performance signal.
options.consequence: At 99.1% the model looks stellar — but the naive predict-never-fraud baseline also hits 99.0%. Accuracy cannot distinguish between a working detector and a model that ignores fraud almost entirely.
options.divergenceCost: Used a metric that cannot discriminate between a useful model and a trivial baseline on imbalanced data.

options.label: Precision, Recall, and PR-AUC (fraud class)
options.detail: Evaluate the model specifically on its ability to find and flag actual fraud cases.
options.consequence: The picture is damning: recall is 8.3% — the model misses 9 out of 10 fraud cases. PR-AUC of 19.4% is barely above the no-skill baseline. Precision at 61% sounds acceptable, but it means nothing if the model almost never fires. Accuracy was hiding a near-useless detector.

artifact.title: Fraud-class metrics: model vs. naive baseline
artifact.caption: Normalized to the fraud class: recall and PR-AUC expose the model as marginally better than doing nothing. Accuracy was masking a near-zero detection rate.

decisions.prompt: Recall is 8.3% and PR-AUC is 19.4%. What do you tell the VP of Risk?

options.label: "This model is broken — don't deploy it, start over."
options.detail: Make a definitive rejection and recommend rebuilding from scratch.
options.consequence: The VP pushes back: 'start over based on what plan?' You've correctly identified the problem but offered no path forward. The team loses confidence in the analysis because it feels like a dead end rather than actionable guidance.
options.divergenceCost: Overclaimed a verdict without pairing it with a diagnostic path or remediation options.

options.label: "Accuracy is misleading here — recall and PR-AUC show the model catches almost no fraud. We should retrain optimizing for PR-AUC and validate with a precision-recall threshold study before any deployment decision."
options.detail: Reframe the evaluation, name the real metrics, and recommend a concrete next step.
options.consequence: The VP now understands why accuracy failed as a signal and has a concrete plan: retrain with a cost-sensitive objective, evaluate on precision-recall curves, and set a recall floor before sign-off. You've turned a near-miss deployment into a well-defined improvement path.

insight: When fraud is ~1% of transactions, a model that predicts 'no fraud' every single time scores 99% accuracy — identical to the deployed model. Accuracy is structurally incapable of measuring minority-class detection on imbalanced data. The right instruments are recall (did we catch the fraud that existed?), precision (when we flagged fraud, were we right?), and PR-AUC (how does that tradeoff look across all thresholds?). The lesson: always ask what a trivially dumb baseline scores before trusting a headline metric.
